summary: PASSporT is a signed token that conveys information about a phone call. This RFC extends it to carry rich call data about the call and the caller, such as a description, that can be signed and protected, sent along, and shown to the person receiving the call.

eli5.summary: When a call comes in, your phone could show who it is and why, and you can trust it wasn't faked. This adds a signed "caller card" to the call.

questions: how to sign caller information in shaken

what is the rcd claim in passport
how does stir sign caller name
subtitle: Signed caller name, icon, jCard and call reason for phone calls, built on PASSporT.

tldr.problem: STIR PASSporT tokens can sign who is calling by number, but the name, icon and other information shown to the called party (the traditional Caller ID) is not protected.
tldr.mechanism: The rich call data (RCD) extension adds the rcd, rcdi and crn claims to PASSporT. Digests in rcdi and JWT Claim Constraints in certificates protect content that is referenced by URL or signed by a non-authoritative party.
tldr.outcome: Call display information can be signed and checked like the calling number, whether it comes from the originating provider or a third party.

today: RFC 9795 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2025 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the PASSporT side of a pair with RFC 9796, which defines the matching SIP Call-Info usage.

sections.title: Signing More Than a Phone Number
sections.content:
PASSporT (RFC 8225) is a token format based on JSON Web Token (JWT) that carries cryptographically signed information about the parties in a communication. Its first use, in RFC 8224, is with SIP. The STIR problem statement left the display name of callers outside its initial scope.

RFC 9795 fills that gap with a PASSporT extension for Rich Call Data (RCD): the traditional Caller ID name plus further caller and call information to be shown to the called party. It protects the SIP display-name and related data such as the Call-Info header field contents. It also covers third-party sources of this data and how to keep its integrity when a non-authoritative party signs.
sections.eli5: Today a signed token proves which number is calling. This adds the name and picture to the sealed envelope, so those cannot be faked either.

sections.title: Four Integrity Modes
sections.content:
The RFC defines three new PASSporT claims. rcd holds the rich call data about the caller. rcdi holds integrity digests. crn is a call reason string, kept separate because it may change on every call, whereas caller information changes less often.

Integrity depends on two questions. Does the RCD include URIs to external content? And is the signer authoritative for the content? That gives four modes. With an authoritative signer and no URIs (mode 1), the normal PASSporT signature is enough. With an authoritative signer and URIs (mode 2), an rcdi claim MUST be included. When the signer is not authoritative (modes 3 and 4), for example a delegate holding a certificate, JWT Claim Constraints in the certificate limit what may be signed, and rcdi is added when URIs are involved.

JWT Claim Constraints come from RFC 8226, extended by RFC 9118. The digest idea is inspired by the W3C Subresource Integrity specification. Delegate certificates are described in RFC 9060.
sections.eli5: If the person who signs the card is the boss of its contents, a normal seal is enough. If a helper signs it, or the card points to pictures stored elsewhere, extra seals prove nothing was swapped.

sections.title: The rcd Claim and Its Keys
sections.content:
The rcd claim is a JSON object with these keys:

  • nam: the display name, matching the SIP display-name syntax. It MUST appear exactly once, and is an empty string if there is no name.
  • apn: an optional alternate presentation number, a canonicalized telephone number the caller is authorized to show instead of their own.
  • icn: an optional HTTPS URL of an image representing the caller, protecting a Call-Info header with purpose icon in SIP.
  • jcd: a jCard JSON object (RFC 7095) included directly.
  • jcl: an HTTPS URL pointing to a jCard JSON object served as application/json.

Only one of jcd or jcl may appear. Their jCard may reference URIs, but that content MUST NOT reference further URIs. The jCard properties follow RFC 9796.

The crn claim is a single optional string matching the call-reason parameter of Call-Info. RFC 9795 also says that jCard data should describe the caller, while claims like crn describe the specific call.
sections.eli5: The caller card has boxes: a name, a number to show, a picture, and a bigger card with more details. The call reason is a sticky note that can change each time.

sections.title: The rcdi Digests and Claim Constraints
sections.content:
Each rcdi entry maps a JSON pointer (RFC 6901) into the rcd claim, such as /icn or /jcd/1/3/3, to a digest of that content. A digest has the form algorithm, a hyphen, then the base64 digest, for example sha256- followed by the encoded value. Implementations MUST support SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, written in lowercase without hyphens.

For JSON values, the input is the JSON serialized with all white space and line breaks removed. For content referenced by a URI, the input is the bytes of the HTTP response body. Every URI in the jCard MUST have its own pointer and digest. For jcl, the key /jcl MUST be present. nam and apn digests are optional because those values are covered by the signature.

In the certificate, the JWT Claim Constraints extension is used so the signer can only produce vetted content. For both claims, it MUST include a mustInclude for rcd, and a mustInclude for rcdi with permittedValues equal to the created rcdi value. Digests are RECOMMENDED over embedding the jCard in the certificate, which is often publicly accessible, for privacy.
sections.eli5: For each picture the card points to, a fingerprint is written down in advance. If someone swaps the picture, the fingerprint no longer matches.

sections.title: Verification, SIP Use and Compact Form
sections.content:
A verifier MUST check the PASSporT signature, the claim construction rules and any JWT Claim Constraints in the certificate. If any check fails, relying parties MUST NOT use any of the claims. Each rcdi digest must match; a failed digest, or an HTTP error while fetching referenced content, means that content is not verified, but SHOULD NOT affect the base PASSporT result for claims included directly. A verifier that does not need to display a URI is NOT RECOMMENDED to fetch it just to check integrity.

In SIP, an authentication service may add the PASSporT extension (ppt) value rcd and the Identity header then carries ppt="rcd". By default nam comes from the From header display-name, or alternatively from P-Asserted-Identity. If it differs from that display-name, the full form of the PASSporT MUST be used. Using Call-Info as a trusted source on the authentication side is NOT RECOMMENDED.

The compact form cannot carry jcl or jcd, and if rcdi is required compact form MUST NOT be used. The rcd, rcdi and crn claims can also be added to a PASSporT of another extension. The RFC's example adds rcd to a shaken PASSporT (RFC 8588) so only one Identity header is needed. A verifier that only knows SHAKEN ignores the rcd claim.
sections.eli5: The phone checks the seal and the fingerprints. If a fingerprint fails, it does not show that part. If it cannot fetch a picture, the rest still works.

sections.title: Third-Party Signers
sections.content:
A service in the call path can ask a third party, such as a name lookup, for rich data. That service acts like a STIR authentication service and creates its own PASSporT, marked with an iss claim. Its credentials do not have authority over the number in orig, and the value of iss MUST reflect the Subject of the signing certificate.

A third-party PASSporT attests information about the calling number, not the call, so its RCD MUST NOT be used when the call has no first-party PASSporT assuring that the number is not spoofed. A verification service MUST check that the orig number matches the call's calling number and that iat is within the usual interval, to prevent cut-and-paste of such a PASSporT into another request. Third-party PASSporTs with RCD are RECOMMENDED to carry iss, and data like crowdsourced reputation scores MUST be in a third-party PASSporT.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a different office, not the phone company, tells you who a number belongs to. Its card is stamped with its own name so you know who is vouching.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Signing RCD should follow a vetting process by an entity that is authoritative, under a policy of the ecosystem using STIR; the policy itself is out of scope. Names, locations and affiliations carry privacy risks. PASSporT has no confidentiality requirement of its own, and transport-level security protects any PASSporT carried in SIP.

Fetching URI-linked resources during verification can reveal calling patterns. Putting RCD constraints into a public certificate may expose information, which is why rcdi digests are RECOMMENDED. Content should be checked when digests are created, for example for unreasonably sized data or recursive URI references, and verifiers should take precautions when fetching it. When delegate certificates are used, constraints should also be considered to stop unauthorized signers from adding other claims.
sections.eli5: A name and picture can say a lot about a person, so the rules ask people to be careful about who can see them and who can change them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA added three claims to the JSON Web Token Claims registry: rcd (Rich Call Data Information), rcdi (Rich Call Data Integrity Information) and crn (Call Reason), all with IETF as change controller. It also added the rcd type to the PASSporT Extensions registry.

A new "PASSporT RCD Claim Types" registry holds the keys allowed in rcd, under Specification Required with expert review. It starts with five names: nam, apn, icn, jcd and jcl.
sections.eli5: The new card box names were written in an official list so nobody else reuses them for something different.

items.label: Display name
items.desc: Required once; empty string if no name.

items.label: Icon URL
items.desc: Optional HTTPS URL of an image.

items.label: jCard link
items.desc: HTTPS URL of a jCard; not together with jcd.
